cau.cau: In 1713, the Treaty of Utrecht gave it to the British Crown "for ever," but "without any territorial jurisdiction, and without any open communication by land."
If Britain ever gave it up, Spain would have first refusal.
The treaty names the town, castle and port, not the sandy isthmus to the north.
Spain says the isthmus was never ceded.
Britain said in 2015 that Gibraltar includes it.

Neither siege took it.

The town behind it is still called La Línea: "the line."

Over two thousand attackers were lost, by a British estimate that includes prisoners, and by a Spanish one; the British rescued three hundred and fifty-seven.

Gibraltar stayed British.

In March 1939, Spain protested that the works stood on "a usurped portion" of its territory.
That November, Spain's foreign minister called the strip a fait accompli, like the Rock itself, while insisting its use breached Spanish territory.
Late in 1939, Britain began a hard runway; in 1941, it was laid across the only road to Spain.

In June 1969, Spain closed the land frontier completely.
It followed Gibraltar's new constitution; a Spanish historian says Madrid applied Utrecht strictly.
Britain counted some four thousand six hundred Spanish day workers cut off.
The gate fully reopened in 1985.

As of 18 October 2026, the treaty is in force only provisionally, pending a European Parliament vote indicated for the fourteenth of December.
